title: Danny DeVito-Produced SXSW Heist Comedy ‘Drag’ Scores Wave of International Sales Out of AFM (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Drag,” the SXSW heist comedy starring Lizzy Caplan and John Stamos and produced by Danny DeVito, has secured a run of international deals followin
body:
“Drag,” the SXSW heist comedy starring Lizzy Caplan and John Stamos and produced by Danny DeVito, has secured a run of international deals following the American Film Market.

	U.K. sales and distribution company Blue Finch Films, which handles the title, has closed Germany with Indeed Film, France with VOD Factory and Spain with A Contracorriente. Poland went to 9th Plan, China to JL Vision and the Middle East and North Africa to Falcon Films, while Penny Black took airline rights. Blue Finch will handle the release itself in the U.K. and Ireland.
	

	In North America, Briarcliff Entertainment holds rights and will open the film in theaters on Jan. 29, 2027.

	From filmmakers Greg Yagolnitzer and Raviv Ullman, “Drag” centers on two sisters who don’t get along and who set out to burgle a remote house in upstate New York. The job goes wrong fast. One sister puts her back out and can’t move from the upper floor, and the pair must find a way out before the owner gets home. Lucy DeVito and Christine Ko round out the cast.

	Danny, Lucy and Jake DeVito produced through Jersey Films 2nd Avenue, the production company they founded, and the film is the company’s first independent feature. The outfit’s earlier credits include FXX animated series “Little Demon” and Amazon sports docuseries “Game 7.” Its new film arm is set up to back original filmmakers and stories that cross genre lines.

	After its premiere at SXSW in 2026, “Drag” went on to play festivals including BiFan, Beyond Fest, Fantasia and Sitges.

	Elsewhere on its slate, Blue Finch is selling “Kick On,” an action horror title that screened in Toronto’s Midnight Madness section, and “Mission,” a George MacKay starrer backed by BBC Film and Screen Scotland.

title: Luca Guadagnino Apologizes for Controversial Costume Design Comments But Defends Working With Fashion Designers: They’re More ‘in Touch With the Pulse of How We Live’
description: Luca Guadagnino apologized to costume designers at the Marrakech Film Festival on Wednesday, a year after drawing backlash for comments he made abo
body:
Luca Guadagnino apologized to costume designers at the Marrakech Film Festival on Wednesday, a year after drawing backlash for comments he made about his preference for working with fashion designers on his films. However, the Italian filmmaker doubled down on his admiration for his frequent collaborator Jonathan Anderson, who most recently designed the costumes for his upcoming Silicon Valley drama “Artificial.”

	“I apologize to costume designers,” Guadagnino said during a conversation at the festival. “There are so many amazing costume designers that I admire so greatly through the history of cinema and contemporary history.”
	

	The controversy dates back to last November, when Guadagnino, speaking with fashion journalist Tim Blanks at the Business of Fashion’s annual VOICES conference, suggested that traditional costume designers were more concerned with the garments themselves than the bodies inhabiting them.

	His comments drew the ire of several prominent costume designers, including Oscar winners Jenny Beavan (“Mad Max: Fury Road,” “Cruella”) and Kate Hawley (“Frankenstein”), who took to the comments section of Business of Fashion’s Instagram post to dispute his characterization of their craft. Beavan wrote at the time, “I can only add I am thankful he will never want to work with me!”

	In Marrakech, Guadagnino further explained his stance.  “It’s just that I like to be in conversation with people who have an immediate touch with the pulse of how we live,” he said.

	Guadagnino singled out Anderson, who, in addition to serving as creative director of Dior, has designed the costumes for three of the filmmaker’s movies: “Challengers,” “Queer” and “Artificial.” “I know he’s someone who sees life in front of him and cares about it,” Guadagnino said of Anderson. “It doesn’t deal with fashion, per se.”
	

	The pair’s latest collaboration, “Artificial,” chronicles the rise of OpenAI and the dramatic ousting and subsequent reinstatement of its CEO Sam Altman in November 2023. The film stars Andrew Garfield as Altman, Yura Borisov as OpenAI co-founder Ilya Sutskever and Ike Barinholtz as Elon Musk.

	“I cannot think of anything more far from an idea of fashion or sophistication or form than Silicon Valley and tech bros,” Guadagnino said. “They actually are gross the way they present themselves.”

	The filmmaker went on to examine how the sartorial codes of the tech industry reflect a broader shift in how the world’s wealthiest and most powerful people communicate their status. “[Anderson] was so smart in understanding every one of these characters and truly never had the temptation of painting something in a better color,” Guadagnino said. 

	“I believe that’s also a language of power,” he continued. “The flip-flops of Zuckerberg are a comfortable item he wears, but also a way for him to indicate his position toward your position.”

	“Artificial,” which had its world premiere at the New York Film Festival in October, will screen at Marrakech Film Festival on Nov. 26. The film will be released by Neon in select theaters on Christmas Day before expanding nationwide on Jan. 8.

schema.headline: Luca Guadagnino Apologizes for Controversial Costume Design Comments But Defends Working With Fashion Designers: They’re More ‘in Touch With the Pulse of How We Live’

title: Hollywood Gets Roasted in Satirical Picture Book ‘We Make a Movie’: ‘I Loved Your Script … Now Change Everything’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
“I loved your script. It is perfect. Now change everything.”

	While probably far from a joke for many screenwriters who have had similar conversat
body:
“I loved your script. It is perfect. Now change everything.”

	While probably far from a joke for many screenwriters who have had similar conversations, this particular line is taken from upcoming satirical picture book “We Make a Movie.”

	Designed to look like a children’s book from the 1960s (particularly the U.K.’s famed “Key Words” educational series by Ladybird), “We Make a Movie” comes from artist Miriam Elia and film industry analyst Stephen Follows and features 20 hand-painted pictures accompanied by short, cheery lines merrily roasting Hollywood and the film industry at large. At the bottom of each are three “new words” to explain what’s really going on (in the case of the script line, the words are “squash,” “original” and “voices”).
	

	“The script says Paris by dawn. The tax break says Eastern Europe,” reads another page likely to make more than a few producers nod knowingly. “‘I loved your film,’ says the sales agent. He has not seen it,” adds another. 

	“Every page comes from something true,” said Follows, who has published more than 600 data-led studies of the industry and is regularly cited in the press. “Anyone in the business will recognize it, and the people it’s about will laugh along without realizing it’s them.”

	Due out next month, “We Make a Movie” has already become something of a hit in the film industry. Pre-orders for the first edition (available to order at www.wemakeamovie.com) are on course to sell out, with a second run being planned.

	“‘We Make a Movie’ is the book of the year — it explains the film industry in a nutshell and in the most entertaining and funny way ever,” said Uwe Boll. “I loved it! A lot of truth to it.”
	

	“We Make a Movie” is already the fastest selling book in Elia’s comedy Dung Beetle series since 2014’s art-world satire “We Go to the Gallery,” which prompted Ladybird owner Penguin books to threaten legal action (she eventually changed names and logos and, following a new copyright law amendment, was able to re-release it). 

	See exclusive spreads from “We Make a Movie” below.

title: AI Horror Short ‘Sikkal’ Wins WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon as Director Promita Banerjee Aims to Make ‘Films With Humans’
description: A horror short rooted in the toll of sickle cell disease on India’s tribal communities has won the inaugural WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon.
body:
A horror short rooted in the toll of sickle cell disease on India’s tribal communities has won the inaugural WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon. 

	Promita Banerjee’s “Sikkal,” made with Google’s AI creative workspace Google Flow, took the INR1.2 million ($12,500) first prize. Syam Manohar’s black comedy “Kuli” placed second, earning INR800,000 ($8,300), and Nikhil Shinde’s animated “Pedals of Joy” came third with INR400,000 ($4,200).


	Women in Film India (WIF India) ran the Filmathon with Google Flow to open up AI filmmaking tools to emerging storytellers around the country. The call drew more than 850 registrations, and a seven-member jury that included directors Shakun Batra and Pan Nalin and Cannes Next head Sten Saluveer narrowed the field to five. The finalists were showcased at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Aamir Khan Productions CEO Aparna Purohit delivered a keynote at the event.
	

	Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant attended the ceremony, where WIF India founder and CEO Guneet Monga Kapoor and filmmaker Ashutosh Gowariker joined the presenters on stage. Srishti Chaudhary’s “Nazar” and Aswathi Naduthodi’s “Bombay Mumbai – Vada Pav” were recognized as finalists.

	“Sikkal” had its beginnings in West Africa, where Banerjee saw how hard sickle cell disease hit families and whole communities. She started developing a project called “Sickle” there with a friend who serves as a UNHCR Goodwill Ambassador, but an emergency pulled her back to India before it went further. Back home, she learned that the disease also weighs heavily on India’s tribal populations, many of whom know little about it and have poor access to treatment.
	

	During her research, a tribal affairs official referred to the disease as “Sikkal,” and Banerjee took the word as her title. Loosely based on one real family, the folk-horror film follows a brother haunted by visions of his dead sister and looks at how poverty and a lack of medical care can leave a child to suffer untreated. Banerjee wants the film to add to the debate around World Sickle Cell Day and the 2027 Global Congress, whose theme focuses on transforming sickle cell care.

	A Kolkata native who grew up in Pondicherry, Banerjee now makes her home in Port Blair in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, where her husband is posted with the Indian Air Force, and divides her time between the islands, Delhi and the Nilgiris. Her grandparents produced Bengali-language films. She started her debut novel, “Songs from Then,” at 29 and saw it published at 44. The book follows women caught up in war and driven from their homes during three uprisings and genocides of the past. A would-be producer who showed interest stripped out its core, then told her to write a screenplay before talking about her vision.

	That exchange pushed her toward filmmaking. At 45 she won a scholarship to the New York Film Academy and went back to the classroom alongside much younger students, later working in New York, Ghana and Japan. Her short “Again Maybe” screened at Ghana’s National Theatre, and another short, “Another Day in Paradise,” sits in the Women Voices Now library.

	“Returning to India, however, was a different story. Somehow, everything began to shrink,” Banerjee said. “Despite the experiences I had accumulated, I found myself outside the industry, without work and, more painfully, without the contacts or networks that are often necessary to find one’s footing.”

	Then she came across WIF India. By that point, she said, AI was all she had left.

	“My personal experience with AI has been deeply moving. I have used it as a companion through my struggles with mental illness, and later, as a creative tool that helped me translate the images in my head into something tangible,” Banerjee said.

	Banerjee now sees “Sikkal” as a calling card for the many stories of hers that remain unmade. “Opaar – The Other Bank,” her first feature, adapted from her novel, is looking for production partners and funding, and she is getting ready to shoot “Faasla,” a segment of an anthology about love and human connection.
	

	“Because, at the end of the day, I want to make films with humans. AI has simply given me a way to begin,” Banerjee said.

	The WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon prizewinners and finalists:

	First prize (INR1.2 million): “Sikkal,” Promita Banerjee (Port Blair) – A folk-horror film about a brother haunted by his late sister, inspired by sickle cell disease among India’s tribal communities.

	Second prize (INR800,000): “Kuli,” Syam Manohar (Kochi) – A black comedy about a nameless man whose giant hole in a village sets tongues wagging. Manohar is co-founder and chief creative officer of Sutra Communications and has worked on more than 500 TV commercials.

	Third prize (INR400,000): “Pedals of Joy,” Nikhil Shinde (Mumbai) – An animated film about Rohan, a balloon seller from a slum who dreams of a sports bike, and Akash, the older brother who tries to help him. Shinde, a Film and Television Institute of India alum, holds an AI director role at Kuku TV.

	Finalist: “Bombay Mumbai – Vada Pav,” Aswathi Naduthodi (Calicut) – A Hindi visual essay that charts the city’s history, from its 1980s mills to the metro, the Sea Link and Marine Drive on the night of the 2011 Cricket World Cup, via people who all reach for the same street snack. Naduthodi, founder of VU Talkies, supervised post-production on Oscar-winning documentary short “The Elephant Whisperers.”

	Finalist: “Nazar,” Srishti Chaudhary (Delhi) – A dialogue-free animated film in which the stares trailing a schoolgirl turn into shadows and watching eyes that follow her even at home. Chaudhary, who studied at NIFT Delhi, co-founded SynimaPro.

schema.headline: AI Horror Short ‘Sikkal’ Wins WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon as Director Promita Banerjee Aims to Make ‘Films With Humans’

title: ‘Ramayana’ Language App Cinedubs Named IFFI Accessibility Partner After Reaching More Than 100,000 Moviegoers in 42 Countries
description: The mobile app that let more than 100,000 moviegoers in 42 countries hear “Ramayana” in a language of their choosing has signed on as accessibility
body:
The mobile app that let more than 100,000 moviegoers in 42 countries hear “Ramayana” in a language of their choosing has signed on as accessibility partner for the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) 2026 in Goa.

	The platform, Cinedubs, has brought its audio description and closed-caption technology to the festival, so that visually impaired and hearing-impaired audiences can watch films in theaters alongside everyone else.


	Nitesh Tiwari’s epic “Ramayana,” starring Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita and Yash as Ravana, opened worldwide on Nov. 5. Cinedubs allowed viewers to pick their own language no matter which version their local cinema was playing, and the company said that service added close to INR40 million ($425,000) to the film’s collections.
	

	The system works through the Cinedubs app. Users download a soundtrack in the language they want and listen through headphones, while the app automatically locks the audio to the film on screen. The same technology carries audio description for visually impaired viewers and closed captions for hearing-impaired viewers.

	“Being chosen as the Accessibility Partner for IFFI 2026 is a moment of immense pride for the entire Cinedubs team,” said Aditya Kashyap, founder of Cinedubs. “We firmly believe that cinema is a universal language and that neither linguistic barriers nor disabilities should prevent anyone from experiencing the power of storytelling.”

	The company pitches its service to filmmakers, producers and distributors as a way to reach audiences they couldn’t previously get to and to earn extra revenue in the process.
	

	Kashyap said the “Ramayana” numbers validated the company’s goal of making cinema borderless. “Accessibility is not just a social responsibility; it is also a significant opportunity for the global film industry to expand its audience base and unlock new revenue streams,” he said.

	During IFFI, Cinedubs plans to meet with filmmakers, production houses, distributors and exhibitors about building a film business that is both more accessible and commercially viable. The company also sees a role in pushing Indian films further into international markets.

	Built by Dubswork Mobile Pvt. Ltd., Cinedubs can be downloaded from both Apple’s and Google’s app stores.

	For cinemas, the app’s multilingual soundtracks run without any changes to existing projection or sound systems.

schema.headline: ‘Ramayana’ Language App Cinedubs Named IFFI Accessibility Partner After Reaching More Than 100,000 Moviegoers in 42 Countries

title: Women Filmmakers From Kyrgyzstan, Romania and Mexico Push Past Tokenism at IFFI Goa
description: Filmmakers from Kyrgyzstan, Romania and Mexico said they want to be recognized for artistic merit rather than token representation, speaking on a p
body:
Filmmakers from Kyrgyzstan, Romania and Mexico said they want to be recognized for artistic merit rather than token representation, speaking on a panel about women in world cinema at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

	Titled “Her Lens, Her Legacy, Her Liberty: Women Shaping World Cinema” and moderated by Indian filmmaker Abhishek Jain, the session brought together Kyrgyz writer-director Narghiza Dotieva, Romanian Roma actress, playwright and filmmaker Alina Șerban and Mexican American writer-director Suzanne Andrews Correa. All three urged emerging filmmakers to stay rooted in their cultural and emotional experiences, arguing that authentic local stories can travel.
	

	Dotieva, whose feature debut “Skylark” explores borderland histories, traced her interest in storytelling to her grandfather’s recitations of “Manas,” the Kyrgyz epic poem. She came to independent filmmaking from advertising and draws on her country’s cultural heritage. She also spoke about the importance of audiences and festivals supporting stories from underrepresented regions.

	Andrews Correa spoke about the decade-long journey of making her debut feature “La Cazadora” (“The Huntress”), which premiered in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the Sundance Film Festival in January. Set in Ciudad Juárez and starring Adriana Paz (“Emilia Pérez”), the film draws on real-life cases of feminicide and on the story of “Diana, the Huntress of Bus Drivers,” the vigilante behind the killings of bus drivers in the city in 2013. Andrews Correa won the Short Film Jury Award at Sundance in 2019 for “Green.”
	

	Șerban, whose directorial feature debut “I Matter” explores Roma identity, faced discrimination growing up in Bucharest. She has used theater and cinema to challenge stereotypes and reclaim Roma narratives, and recalled funding rejections because her scripts did not fit conventional portrayals of the community.

	Șerban also described her presence at IFFI as an emotional return to an ancestral homeland, pointing to the historical links between the Roma community and Rajasthan in northwest India.

schema.headline: Women Filmmakers From Kyrgyzstan, Romania and Mexico Push Past Tokenism at IFFI Goa

title: Vijay Sethupathi’s ‘Maharaja’ Producer Confirms Hollywood Remake Approach as WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Weighs Whether Indian IP Can Travel
description: The success in China of Tamil thriller “Maharaja” has led to an approach from a Hollywood agency for remake rights, producer Sudhan Sundaram confir
body:
The success in China of Tamil thriller “Maharaja” has led to an approach from a Hollywood agency for remake rights, producer Sudhan Sundaram confirmed during a panel at WAVES Film Bazaar, the market held alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, where the film was held up as an example of the growing reach of Indian film intellectual property (IP).

	Produced by Sundaram, the Chennai-based founder of Passion Studios, the 2024 Vijay Sethupathi starrer reportedly grossed approximately INR910 million ($9.6 million) at the Chinese box office.
	

	Titled “From Local Hit to Global IP: Rooted in India, Reimagined for the World” and moderated by Rajeev Masand, the panel featured Nikhil Madhok, director and head of originals at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios India; Saugata Mukherjee, head of content at Yash Raj Entertainment; Ruchikaa Kapoor Sheikh, director at Netflix India; and Paolo Teta, head of business affairs at LSPG. The speakers commended the success of “Maharaja.”

	“The fact that we are talking about whether Indian stories are truly traveling tells you something, which is that we still haven’t had that global moment where something is consistently traveling,” Madhok said. “What we see with Korean content, that breakthrough moment hasn’t happened for India yet. The journey has begun, and we’re well on the path to doing that.”

	Authentic, locally rooted stories have a better chance of standing out internationally than those derived from existing formats or trends, Madhok said, citing Prime Video series “Made in Heaven” and “Raakh” as shows that had traveled beyond expectations.
	

	For Kapoor Sheikh, India has always been a storytelling powerhouse, and streaming has made language less of a barrier. “Revenge, love, first love, heartbreak, a mother’s love for a child – these are so universal that we’re hoping the audience comes back to that world to continue exploring it. What, therefore, is local and what is global? That’s something to question,” she said.

	Mukherjee pointed out that Indian films such as “Mother India” (1957) and “Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge” (1995) have traveled internationally for decades. With streaming, he said, the lines between local and global have started to blur, and the distinction now is between a story finding viewers abroad and its IP being adapted or remade for other markets. “Have the IPs traveled? Have we got a show which is being remade into 50 other languages? Not yet,” he said.

	The discussion also turned to franchises and the risk of losing sight of the standalone film. Madhok said the first priority must be to make a compelling film and establish its characters, with an extension following only if there is another worthwhile story to tell. Mukherjee agreed that a franchise should be driven by story rather than the commercial appeal of extending a hit, suggesting that some stories draw their strength from remaining contained.

	The panel also identified animation as an opportunity for Indian storytelling, given the country’s wealth of folk narratives and cultural traditions.

	Teta argued that understanding the legal and commercial framework early need not constrain creativity and can help filmmakers make informed decisions about the future use of their work. He also suggested that agreements should find ways to recognize and reward original writers if a property is later adapted.

	“Come to the lawyer early. If you come late it might be too late and expensive for you,” Teta told producers, urging them to weigh adaptation and remake rights when rights are acquired or a project is commissioned.

schema.headline: Vijay Sethupathi’s ‘Maharaja’ Producer Confirms Hollywood Remake Approach as WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Weighs Whether Indian IP Can Travel

title: Generative AI Indian Feature ‘Maharaja in Denims,’ Inspired by Sikh Ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Sets April 2027 Release (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “Maharaja in Denims,” author Khushwant Singh’s novel about a young man who relives the life of 19th-century Sikh ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, is ne
body:
“Maharaja in Denims,” author Khushwant Singh’s novel about a young man who relives the life of 19th-century Sikh ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, is nearing the finish line as a feature-length generative AI film – one its makers say they effectively had to make three times.

	The team hopes to release the film by April 2027, in time for Baisakhi, the Punjabi harvest festival. Ahmedabad-based Twenty-Twenty One Studios has come aboard as co-producer and is weighing a theatrical run followed by non-theatrical distribution. Balpreet Kaur, a Punjab-based independent filmmaker, is directing and holds final creative control.
	

	The book was optioned in July 2020 by producer Guneet Monga Kapoor, but that version never got made. Singh, who is also CEO of Intelliflicks Studios, the company producing the AI film, tells Variety the timing worked against it. The option landed in the middle of the COVID pandemic, cinemas were slow to recover, and a story spanning Ranjit Singh’s reign as well as 20th- and 21st-century India was always going to be a costly gamble for a producer.

	The AI route came from Gurdeep Pall, then corporate VP of incubations at Microsoft. During a visit to Chandigarh in 2023, Pall asked Singh why the book had never reached the screen and proposed trying it with generative AI. His work with OpenAI’s models had convinced him the technology would mature within a couple of years to the point where a realistic feature was possible.

	“It has unfolded exactly as predicted,” Singh says.

	The pair co-founded Intelliflicks that year and unveiled the project with a short clip in 2024.
	

	Choosing realism over mythology or sci-fi made consistency the central problem. Production began in 2024 with Midjourney and Runway, shifted to Google Veo, with Nano Banana handling stills, then moved through Kling AI and Seedance 2.0 before wrapping on tools available on Higgsfield. ChatGPT and Google Imagen helped build early character references, and keeping faces, costumes and sets in line took heavy manual fixes with face-swapping software, Photoshop and Adobe Firefly.

	Nano Banana proved the turning point, letting the team generate new camera angles and compositions from reference images with far fewer manual corrections. Even so, Singh says near-perfect shot-to-shot consistency only became achievable four or five months ago. The team rebuilt the stills for the entire film three times before locking a look. When Higgsfield began allowing moving shots to be generated straight from character sheets, switching over would have added time and money, so the team animated the stills it already had.

	Performances went through a similar evolution. Early on, real actors guided them via Runway Act-One. A single person created most of the motion shots so that each character would speak, move and react the same way throughout. The short clips also gave the editor less room to shape scenes than conventional footage allows.

	“For example, if a lampshade is placed at a particular spot in a two-minute scene, it must remain in exactly the same position across every generated shot, irrespective of the camera angle. Even the slightest inconsistency can disrupt the cinematic experience,” Singh says.

	That learning curve drove up the budget. Singh says new technology usually cuts costs to around a tenth, but the team redid close to an hour of the film three times as the tools improved. He puts the cost at more than $500,000, excluding marketing, which has yet to begin.

	“Throughout this technological evolution, the creative process has remained entirely human-led. Screenwriting, direction, storyboarding, shot composition, performance evaluation and final creative decisions remain with our filmmaking team. AI is the technology that helps us translate that vision onto the screen,” Singh says.

	Set in 2008, the film follows Hari Sandhu, who has flashbacks to three earlier lives: as Ranjit Singh, as a victim of Partition violence in 1947 and as a victim of the 1984 anti-Sikh violence. Kaur chose pivotal episodes from Ranjit Singh’s life and added material from outside the novel to give his story more screen heft. The team stuck closely to historical sources, Singh says, but took liberties where the tools couldn’t render period costumes accurately. Keeping faces and headgear consistent was also a major hurdle when production began, and some early imagery still bears the marks. Singh vetted the screenplay for accuracy with input from historians, but leaves day-to-day filmmaking to Kaur.
	

	The AI film joins a long line of Ranjit Singh projects. Last week, Katha Studios and B4 Makers Studios unveiled a big-screen biopic of the ruler, set to shoot in 2027. Actor-politician Raj Babbar’s series “Maharaja Ranjit Singh” ran on public broadcaster Doordarshan from 2010 to 2011, while Contiloe Pictures’ “Sher-e-Punjab: Maharaja Ranjit Singh,” with Damanpreet Singh in the title role, aired on Life OK in 2017. Feature versions have proved harder to get off the ground. Babbar’s planned film “The Lord of Five Rivers: Maharaja Ranjit Singh” was shelved, and “Border” director J.P. Dutta lined up a Ranjit Singh biopic after his 2018 war film “Paltan.” Ranjit Singh’s son Duleep Singh, the last Sikh maharaja, was the subject of Kavi Raz’s 2017 feature “The Black Prince,” starring Satinder Sartaaj.

	The music is entirely human-made. Every song was written, composed and performed by people, and dubbing and narration were recorded with actors in the studio. Playback singer Sukhwinder Singh sang two versions of the title track, composed by up-and-coming singer Hargun Kaur, after the team also considered Rahat Fateh Ali Khan, Wazir Patar and Daler Mehndi. Recorded in Mumbai, the track pairs modern production with traditional instruments of 19th-century Punjab. Internet sensation Inayat Kaur Bajaj makes her film debut, Punjab-based Azaad and Gurprasad Singh composed and performed several tracks, and the lyricists include Harmanjit Singh, known for “Rani Tatt,” as well as Ferro Fluid, Azaad and director Kaur.

	On copyright, Singh relays Pall’s view that there are two separate questions. What data the AI models were trained on is one for the companies that own them. How Intelliflicks uses those models is the studio’s responsibility, and it avoids drawing on any style or IP that belongs to a person or company.

	Singh pushes back on concerns that AI filmmaking will put actors, animators and other crew out of work, pointing to a century of the industry adopting new tools, VFX among them.

	“Having made this film we see a need for human creativity and talent, from storytelling to cinematography to music. Sometimes the specific roles change but human involvement will be needed to make compelling cinema with AI,” he says.

	Glitches may remain, Singh concedes, but he likens them to the flaws of the earliest motion pictures.
	

	“I definitely see ‘Maharaja in Denims’ as an experiment, and a successful one at that, because technically, it will be the first full-length generative AI film rooted in realism, and it will be there for everyone to see,” he says.

	Intelliflicks is already exploring an adaptation of Singh’s next novel, “The Opium Toffee,” a love story set in Punjab during the 1980s, and has a spy script and a war film in development. The company is also open to partnering with outside filmmakers on hybrid productions.

schema.headline: Generative AI Indian Feature ‘Maharaja in Denims,’ Inspired by Sikh Ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Sets April 2027 Release (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Mike Newell Recalls Being Shot at in Colombia While Filming ‘Love in the Time of Cholera’ With Giovanna Mezzogiorno: ‘She Was Like, “F— All This!”’
description: This year’s Torino Film Festival opened with a valentine to British artists, as directors Stephen Frears and Mike Newell collected lifetime achieve
body:
This year’s Torino Film Festival opened with a valentine to British artists, as directors Stephen Frears and Mike Newell collected lifetime achievement awards ahead of a screening of “November 1963,” the latest from Palme d’Or winner Roland Joffé.

	Of the same generation, the three filmmakers followed remarkably similar paths. All cut their teeth on the BBC’s landmark 1970s anthology series “Play for Today” before breaking into the big league with a string of 1980s and ’90s classics, including “The Mission,” “The Killing Fields,” “Dangerous Liaisons,” “The Grifters,” “Four Weddings and a Funeral” and “Donnie Brasco.”
	

	So when Newell took the stage to accept his Stella della Mole trophy, he began by paying tribute to a friendship that took root at the University of Cambridge in the early 1960s. 

	“It’s lovely to be in the same hall as my old friend Stephen Frears, whom I have known since I was 18 years old,” he said to booming applause. “We go a ways back.” 

	Accepting his award from Italian actress Giovanna Mezzogiorno, Newell also recalled the less-than-ideal conditions surrounding their 2007 collaboration, “Love in the Time of Cholera,” which was shot in Colombia, with Javier Bardem, Liev Schreiber and Benjamin Bratt also in the cast.



	

					Giovanna Mezzogiorno in “Love in the Time of Cholera”
									Courtesy of New Line Cinema
	



	“She and I made a movie in impossible circumstances, in an impossible country, of an impossible script,” he quipped. “And we managed to live through it!” It wasn’t always easy, he added, particularly when the crew found themselves in a helicopter unable to land because of ground fire. “They were shooting at us, and [the pilot] just didn’t want to go,” Newell recalled. “There was Giovanna Mezzogiorno, on my arm, being shot at, being like, ‘F— all this!'” 
	

	Frears, meanwhile, drew plenty of laughs by thumbing post-Brexit wounds. “I’m English,” he reminded the Turin crowd. “Do you remember England? Once we were European!”

	Now readying on his 25th theatrical feature, the director was equally self-effacing about his prolific career. “[Directing is] all I can do,” he deadpanned. “I can’t do anything else. I’m helpless.” Still, the work has brought him plenty of pleasure. “I’ve always had a good time,” he admitted. “I mean, look at those actors [with whom I’ve worked]. I’ve been very lucky.”



	

					Carlo Chatrian and Stephen Frears 
									Torino Film Festival
	



	Alongside a tribute to Margarethe von Trotta, the first female director to win the Golden Lion for 1981’s “Marianne and Juliane,” the opening ceremony also doubled as a stealth “Pulp Fiction” reunion, with John Travolta and Maria de Medeiros both receiving lifetime achievement trophies.

	Though the actors shared little screen time in the 1994 Palme d’Or winner, they more than made up for it in Turin. At the festival’s opening dinner, Travolta greeted de Medeiros with a warm embrace and declared: “You and I made history.”

	Accepting her award in fluent Italian, the Portuguese actress offered a few thoughts on the relationship between language and performance. 

	“Every language has its own point of view, but I have to say that Italian was a dream for me, and I learned it while filming ‘The Remains of Nothing’ with Antonietta De Lillo in Naples. I had a wonderful coach for Italian, and for Neapolitan there were 15, all with different opinions!” 

	“This prize is an absolute landmark,” de Medeiros continued. “I’m truly honored to receive this star alongside so many extraordinary names in cinema, and we all also want to celebrate Italian cinema, which is a reference point for filmmakers all over the world.”



	

					Alberto Cirio, Maria de Medeiros, Giulio Base 
									Torino Film Festival

schema.headline: Mike Newell Recalls Being Shot at in Colombia While Filming ‘Love in the Time of Cholera’ With Giovanna Mezzogiorno: ‘She Was Like, “F— All This!”’

title: Cole Sprouse Says He Didn’t Make ‘Substantial Money’ on ‘Riverdale’ Until Season 4: TV Is ‘Not as Profitable for Actors Anymore’
description:
Cole Sprouse is getting candid about the realities of being a TV actor. 

	During an appearance on his brother Dylan Sprouse’s “Wildmen” podcast —
body:
Cole Sprouse is getting candid about the realities of being a TV actor. 

	During an appearance on his brother Dylan Sprouse’s “Wildmen” podcast — which marked the “Suite Life of Zack & Cody” stars’ first on-screen reunion in a decade — Cole reflected on his time starring on the teen drama series from 2017 to 2023 and how television has changed.

	“‘Riverdale‘ was kind of a dying species at the time because it was as we were transitioning into the streaming model, so we would film 22 hour-long episodes a year,” Cole said (via Entertainment Weekly). 
	

	He explained that a typical TV contract is fixed for the first three years, and then allows for renegotiations. “So you are making what you initially agreed upon, and if the show is a success and they want to pick it up for a fourth season, you get the option to renegotiate after the third season,” he continued. “So that’s when you start making money. Substantial money. If the show is a big success, that’s when you start actually being able to roll in it.”

	Cole, who has mainly worked in film since “Riverdale,” added that TV is just not as lucrative as it once was. 

	“If a show is a success, regardless, across the board, it is a great launching pad and vehicle for the future of anyone’s career,” he said. “However, the days of cutting your teeth in relative anonymity and making your bag and getting your 10,000 hours on a long-running, consistent, stable work in television is gone. It’s not as profitable a medium itself anymore, and it’s just not as profitable for actors anymore.”
	

	Elsewhere in the episode, Cole and Dylan also discussed the effect being child stars had on them. In addition to “Suite Life,” the twins starred together in “Friends,” “Big Daddy” and the spinoff “Suite Life on Deck.” 

	“What happens a lot with us, which I find very interesting, is that when people come up as fans — which is always flattering — they’ll make sure to let you know which one of you is their favorite,” Dylan said.

	Added Cole, “I will say that that used to do a lot of damage to us when we were kids. All the comparison, oh my God.” 

	Watch the full “Wildmen” episode below.

title: Taylor Swift's Former Music Teacher Speaks Out After Vanity Fair Comments
description:
Taylor Swift's Ex Music Teacher
                          My Vanity Fair Interview Was Positive .
body:
Taylor Swift's Ex Music Teacher
                          My Vanity Fair Interview Was Positive ...
                          They Took It Out of Context
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Taylor Swift's former music teacher, who spoke about the singer to Vanity Fair, says she thinks highly of Taylor … despite what the article shared. 
      
    
              Sharon Luyben, who taught at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High for three decades, tells TMZ ... "All I said were positive things." 
      
    
              She tells us Taylor was a "fabulous student" and adds, "I was also a neighbor and friend with her parents who were very nice and active in our community."
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Vanity Fair did not use quotes from Sharon speaking highly of Taylor … instead, it used only one quote from her denying Taylor's claim that people didn't want to sit with her at lunch … and would move away from her. 
      
    
              Sharon told the reporter students had assigned seating at lunch … and, as such, Taylor's claim didn't make sense. Another student backed up the claim … while a second student the outlet spoke to wasn't sure. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              The music teacher isn't the only one clearing the air after the article..
      
    
              Taylor's former classmate, Arielle Peppers, told us she wasn't trying to throw shade when she recalled a story about Taylor's expensive Ugg boots.
      
    
              As you know, Vanity Fair dropped a scathing profile of Taylor on Monday ... taking aim at her carefully cultivated image, personal relationships, and alleged industry feuds ... though she's reportedly not letting it get to her.

              Kamala Harris may have her eyes on the White House again ... but for now, she's got her sights set on some high fashion in Paris.
      
    
              The former vice president and her husband, Doug Emhoff, were spotted at a Chanel boutique over the weekend ... taking a little retail therapy break before the 2028 presidential race starts heating up.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
              Photos obtained by TMZ show Harris and Emhoff relaxing on a couch inside the luxury store, surrounded by designer clothing and several people who appear to be assisting them. There's snacks and glasses of Champagne in front of them, too.
      

              No word on whether she walked away with any pricey purchases ... but she certainly looked right at home.
      
    
              The fashionable outing comes as Harris keeps the door open on another presidential run ... saying she's considering another shot at the White House in 2028 after losing to Donald Trump in 2024.
      
    
              For now, Kamala's trading campaign stops for Chanel shops ... and keeping her options open for 2028.
